Yes. The ending pays off the story's central theme of attention as generosity (Weil) and the narrator's arc from needing to be seen to being able to see. The final scene mirrors the first seminar. Back then she spoke and was asked to "say more." Now she stays silent and listens, an unwitnessed generosity that echoes Johan's night baking.

The other threads are resolved before this closing beat:
- Carl leaves kindly.
- Lizzy apologizes with the fallen cake.
- Martin is seen diminished in the reading room.
- Johan teaches the narrator to exist without a witness.

The last line delivers the moment the whole piece has been building toward, so the ending feels purposeful rather than abrupt.
